Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back to the all-important run chase. The umpires are already out to the center as the Australian players take their respective fielding positions. The opening pair of Tammy Beaumont and Maia Bouchier walk out to the crease for England Women. Megan Schutt has the new ball as the countdown goes off. A regular slip in readiness. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Well then, a low-scoring clash in Sydney, and now the same at Melbourne. Australia has a score way below-par, and now the bowlers will have to crack the code to run through the English batting lineup with effect. However, England's batting order didn't perform well either in the previous game and despite of 181 to chase, coupled with a bowling attack like Australia, they would definitely feel the pressure. Do not go anywhere, as the run chase begins in just a few minutes.

England came out much improved in the fielding department this time around which further put the squeeze on. It was the phase between 31-40 overs where England really pressed on Australia, giving just 22 runs in that phase, while spin domination was at full tilt along with three more wickets. Alana King did try to resist but only for a brief period. But after her departure, England went on for the kill and prevented Australia from batting their allotted 50 overs. It was a total spin dominance as Sophie Ecclestone and Alice Capsey shared seven wickets between them, with the former snagging an impactful 4-fer, while Lauren Bell got a coupe as well.

What followed was a dramatic collapse that saw Australia stumble from a position of strength at 131/2 to a precarious 150/6 in approximately seven overs. The slide began with Ecclestone's breakthrough, before Alice Capsey took center stage with a brilliant three-wicket haul. The Australian innings was further dented when Lauren Filer returned to dismiss the dangerous Tahlia McGrath, adding to the visitors' woes.

With the pitch offering significant grip and turn, Heather Knight astutely introduced her spin attack in tandem. The combination of Ecclestone partnering with Capsey and Dean proved too hot to handle on a turning track.  The run flow, which had been smooth until then, began to dry up as boundaries became increasingly difficult to find. The dismissal of the well-set half-centurion Ellyse Perry during this period was particularly crucial, leaving Australia in a worrisome position.

The second phase saw Litchfield growing in confidence as she built a promising partnership with Ellyse Perry. As the movement diminished and batting became easier, both batters settled into a rhythm, preferring to accumulate runs through smart cricket rather than aggressive stroke play. However, Sophie Ecclestone, with her uncanny knack for breaking partnerships, lived up to her reputation by dismissing Litchfield in her very first over, breaking the 49-run stand for the second wicket. This set of ten overs saw Australia accumulating another 53 runs.

England's decision to bowl first on a greenish surface didn't yield immediate dividends as the Lauren pair - Filer and Bell - struggled to find their rhythm early on. This allowed the Australian openers to capitalize on any loose deliveries. While Alyssa Healy took on the aggressive role, Phoebe Litchfield weathered a testing period where the ball kept low at one end. The opening partnership looked threatening until Lauren Bell finally broke through, having Healy caught behind. Australia ended the powerplay at 53/1, largely dominating the early exchanges.

A job well done by the English side with the ball as they effectively reduced Australia from 131/2 to 180 all out. What unfolded in the middle overs was a perfect example of a domino effect as once the spinners created pressure and found their first breakthrough, the Australian middle order crumbled in succession, with no batter able to establish themselves at the crease. It was a stark contrast to their powerplay dominance.

As far as the pitch is concerned, this is one track that offers good purchase for the spinners than any other track in this part of the world. Hence, the likes of Alana King, Ash Gardner from Australia, Sophie Ecclestone and Sarah Glenn from the English camp might come pretty handy here. With all said, can England bounce back against the odds? Or will Australia dominate again? A lot to play for with two crucial points up for grabs. Do not go anywhere as we bring the toss and team updates in just a bit.

This hasn't been a venue known for high-scoring affairs, with the highest first innings total falling short of 200. The ground has particularly favored Australia in their head-to-head encounters with England, where they've maintained an unblemished record in both previous meetings. In fact, Australia's dominance at this venue extends beyond just England matches, as they've emerged victorious in all nine games they've played here.

England find themselves in a race against time with a swift turnaround between matches, facing the challenge of bouncing back. Their position was compromised early when they posted a below-par total, forcing them to play the catch-up. The pressure was further amplified by several fielding lapses that proved costly in a contest where margins for error are minimal, particularly given the intensity of this storied rivalry. Despite the batting struggles, there were glimpses of fightback in their bowling. Lauren Filer and Sophie Ecclestone managed to create breakthroughs during the middle overs, showcasing their ability to challenge even well-set batters. However, England's primary concern lies in their batting department, as many batters managed to establish themselves at the crease but failed to convert these promising starts into substantial contributions, a trend they'll need to address urgently.

The hosts flexed their muscles at the Showgrounds, where their bowling attack operated like a well-oiled machine to stifle England's batting ambitions. Every bowler made meaningful impact with the ball. The standout performance came from the ever-reliable Ashleigh Gardner, who showcased her all-round brilliance with both bat and ball. However, there’s a minor wrinkle which the hosts would like to iron it out. While the hosts' performance was largely impressive, their middle-order showed signs of vulnerability during the chase, experiencing a noticeable dip in momentum when they lost quick wickets through the middle overs. But the modest target set by England meant these batting hiccups didn't prove costly, allowing the hosts to navigate to victory with relative comfort.

Welcome to the Junction Oval in Melbourne, where the Women's Ashes intensity reaches new heights as Australia and England prepare to face each other in the second ODI. With the series momentum tilted a bit in Australia's favor after their commanding performance in the opener, this match promises to be a fascinating contest, as England waits eagerly to find an equaliser.

The 2025 cricketing calendar has started off with a bang with al lot of international action to go along with the different T20 Leagues across the global but now it is time to focus on the biggest rivalry in Women's cricket as Australia Women play host to England Women in the 2025 Women's Ashes which will be played across all three formats of the game and a point system will decide which side will take the bragging rights. We have the three-game ODI up first and the hosts have already taken a 1-0 lead thanks to a victory at the North Sydney Oval. The second match will take place at the Junction Oval and England Women will be eager to hit back and level up the series. In Sydney, the surface seemed like a belted but there was some swing and up and down bounce for the pacers and then, the spinners got a fair bit of purchase as well which made it difficult to start with the bat. The English batters fell prey to not kicking on once getting an eye in and played a few loose shots which were forced upon by some really tight bowling from the Aussies. Eventually a few individuals contributions took England Women over the 200 run mark but it seemed below par. Chasing 205 for the win, Australia Women had a shaky start themselves and lost the likes of Phoebe Litchfield and Ellyse Perry as Lauren Bell and Lauren Filer bowled top opening spells. Sophie Ecclestone always seemed in the game but skipper Alyssa Healy made sure that she didn't let a promising start go to waste. However, she fell in the 80s, leaving the door slightly ajar and the visitors almost made a match out of it but Ash Gardner kept a cool head and took them over the line. If that experienced English top order gets going, things could be quite different in the second ODI and on the whole, the bowling front both sides was brilliant and it was more a matter of a couple of individuals stepping up with the bat for the Aussies. It should be yet another cracking contest and we get to watch it with comfort. Who are you backing for the win?
